title: Talking AI for Access to Justice at the 25th Innovations in Technology Conference — full episode transcript
pub: Talk Justice, Legal Services Corporation / Legal Talk Network
author: Sateesh Nori · Lisa Colpoys

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source shifts the focus from AI’s threat to associate expertise reproduction toward access to justice, legal-aid capacity and smaller practices. It acknowledges employment fears and automation of routine burdens but does not substantively address the verification–experience paradox or propose reconstructed apprenticeship; instead, it prioritises using AI to expand affordable legal help and reserve lawyers’ time for human work.
qs: And I think that’s the model that we have to embrace a place in which there are more options for work for people in our field and more opportunities for people who seek legal services to get that help because it’ll be more widely available, more specialized and cheaper.
We can free up time by allowing AI to help with those things and do the things that only humans can do.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source does not directly accept the cluster’s framing that automation threatens apprenticeship and partner succession or endorse explicit funding, simulation and feedback as remedies. Instead, it proposes a different operating model: AI-enabled, smaller and more specialized practices that deepen expertise, broaden career options and expand affordable legal access. These remain forecasts rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: We can really do that going forward and that’s going to help each of those people who are going to feel more skilled or develop their skills deeper and become experts and not generalists.

And I think that’s the model that we have to embrace a place in which there are more options for work for people in our field and more opportunities for people who seek legal services to get that help because it’ll be more widely available, more specialized and cheaper.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that AI will reshape legal-service production and provider structures rather than eliminate lawyers. It materially extends that proposition with a concrete access-to-justice model: automate small-practice administration to support neighborhood-based, issue-specific providers offering cheaper, more widely available help. Its 2030 claims remain explicitly speculative rather than evidence-backed.
qs: All of those things can be automated by ai.

And I think that’s the model that we have to embrace a place in which there are more options for work for people in our field and more opportunities for people who seek legal services to get that help because it’ll be more widely available, more specialized and cheaper.

st.t: Civil justice: Capacity gains need human safeguards
st.an: The source endorses AI as a means to expand legal-aid capacity by reducing intake, triage and administrative burdens while reserving substantive, human-dependent work for lawyers. It also supports timely, needs-led deployment for people otherwise receiving no help, while presenting anticipated benefits and practitioner estimates rather than measured legal outcomes.
qs: And for the first time in my career, I’m seeing a path forward out of the kind of mess of intake and triage that we’re all stuck in a way forward that allows us to do that type of work that only we can do.
Not perfect, perfect is the enemy of the good, but no help versus really good help.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s claim that AI-driven reductions in production time pressure hourly funding and require a broader reconsideration of how client value is funded. It also supports experimentation while acknowledging job insecurity and professional risk aversion, but offers anecdotal reasoning rather than evidence or a material extension of the cluster’s delivery model.
qs: If funding is based on the number of hours people spend doing certain kinds of work, and this technology undercuts that, then it’s not just rethinking the billable hour, but it’s rethinking how we acknowledge and fund value and service that is created for clients, right?
What I strive to do with my students is replace that fear with curiosity.

st.t: Justice augmentation: Activity exceeds proven access gains
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s augmentation framing: AI may relieve intake and triage burdens while preserving lawyers’ distinctive human work. It also reinforces the synthesis’s evidentiary caution because its reported experimentation is qualitative and does not demonstrate improved access or legal outcomes, while advocating community-needs research and procurement support for responsible adoption.
qs: And for the first time in my career, I’m seeing a path forward out of the kind of mess of intake and triage that we’re all stuck in a way forward that allows us to do that type of work that only we can do.
Understanding what people need and want and where they are as a foundational matter.

st.t: Justice capacity: AI potential requires deliberate implementation
st.an: The source supports the proposition that AI may expand justice capacity but that current evidence is prospective and implementation-dependent. Nori identifies a possible route through intake and triage bottlenecks, while Moon reports encouraging experimentation—especially with user support—without measured service or access outcomes.
qs: They found that those, especially those who had some help, some concierge service, learning how to use the tools and deploy them effectively in their work, did some really cool stuff.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source accepts that AI could expand legal help and staff capacity, while treating those benefits as prospective and contingent on careful pilots, human-centred needs assessment, accuracy safeguards, procurement guidance and sustainable funding. Its concern that efficiency could undermine hours-based funding reinforces the cluster’s conclusion that uptake alone cannot close the justice gap.
qs: Lisa Colpoys:  I think that, and we’re really focusing on how AI can help legal aid organizations and legal aid lawyers do their work better, be more efficient, help more people.

If funding is based on the number of hours people spend doing certain kinds of work, and this technology undercuts that, then it’s not just rethinking the billable hour, but it’s rethinking how we acknowledge and fund value and service that is created for clients, right?

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s view that AI adoption is organizational change rather than a simple technology purchase. It advocates incremental, measurable implementation that brings colleagues along, recognizes professional fear and risk aversion, and identifies funding structures as an incentive that may need redesign. Its access-to-justice focus is narrower than the cluster but consistent with its principal proposition.
qs: We have to think in terms of baby steps and progress that is measurable and verifiable and we can bring everyone along with us.

If funding is based on the number of hours people spend doing certain kinds of work, and this technology undercuts that, then it’s not just rethinking the billable hour, but it’s rethinking how we acknowledge and fund value and service that is created for clients, right?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The panel strongly supports selective, human-led deployment: AI should handle bounded administrative work while lawyers retain counselling, collaboration and trial work, with outputs tested and verified for their intended purpose. Its incremental change-management approach aligns with operating-model redesign, although Nori’s unsupported prediction that AI will collapse corporate law’s billable-hour model is more deterministic than the synthesis.
qs: But we can let the AI do the things that it is good at so we can have the time to do those things.
What we have to do is trust it, test it, verify it, make sure that it’s accurate for the purpose that we’re using it for.

kp.k: Supported experimentation informs legal aid AI adoption
kp.d: Host Cat Moon reports an earlier study giving about a hundred people in legal aid organizations paid ChatGPT access for open-ended experimentation. She characterizes results as extraordinary, particularly for participants receiving concierge assistance with using the tools. The transcript provides no quantified outcomes or detailed study design.
qs: They put in the hands of people, about a hundred people, access to the paid versions of chat GPT, and just let people go to see what they could do, what they could build, and the results were pretty extraordinary.
They found that those, especially those who had some help, some concierge service, learning how to use the tools and deploy them effectively in their work, did some really cool stuff.

kp.k: Illinois initiative builds shared adoption infrastructure
kp.d: Lisa Colpoys describes the Lawyers Trust Fund of Illinois AI initiative, operating since September, as support for legal aid organizations exploring and deploying AI. Discovery included discussions with most of its 55 grantees and a staff survey establishing a baseline. Existing support includes weekly office hours, a statewide discussion group with about 150 signups, and a five-webinar series covering introductions, prompting, use policies and ethics. Planned resources include peer learning and procurement guidance developed with pro bono counsel.
qs: there’s 55 grantees that Lawyers Trust Fund has
but also to set a baseline to collect some data so that we know where we’re starting.
We also have an AI discussion group that’s statewide. We’re with about 150 people who’ve signed up already
So when legal aid leaders begin to purchase AI technology, they’ll have a roadmap and a checklist they can use.

kp.k: Administrative automation could redirect scarce legal aid capacity
kp.d: Sateesh Nori grounds his argument in personal experience: over 22 years in New York City legal services, he estimates representing a thousand clients and turning away more than 10,000 people. He asserts that operational questions consume more than half of practitioners' time and energy, including intake, translation, filing and accessible rights materials. He presents AI as a way to reduce those burdens and reserve lawyers' intelligence, creativity and skill for substantive legal problems; these are experiential claims and anticipated benefits, not measured productivity findings.
qs: I probably represented a thousand clients.
I probably turned away more than 10,000 people during that time.
And I realized that how questions are taking up more than half of our time and energy, they’re burning us out.
Those are the questions that require our intelligence and creativity and skill.

kp.k: Roxanne targets unmet tenant repair needs directly
kp.d: Nori reports launching Roxanne AI on January 7th after 13 months of work, one week before the discussion. The tenant-facing chatbot supplies natural-language information about housing conditions. He argues that New York City's eviction-focused lawyers and emergency-case queues leave repair problems inadequately served. He expressly acknowledges uncertainty about a direct-to-consumer launch, including accuracy, trust and unauthorized-practice issues; no user outcomes are reported.
qs: last week on January 7th, after 13 months of work, we launched a tool called Roxanne.
So Roxanne AI is a tenant facing chatbot.
We have a lot of issues to navigate around unauthorized practice of law and accuracy and trust.
When we release something that goes directly to the consumer, we have no idea what’s going to happen. It’s only been a week.
One reason is the lawyers are focused on evictions. They don’t have time to address things like lack of heat or mold or lead paint.

kp.k: Actionable information proposed to navigate unauthorized-practice constraints
kp.d: Nori proposes 'actionable legal information' as an intermediate category between legal information and legal advice that could navigate unauthorized-practice restrictions. This is his proposed interpretation, not a reported regulatory approval or legal holding. He connects earlier access to usable information with preventing downstream legal crises; Moon separately frames this as a shift from the profession's reactive orientation toward proactive assistance.
qs: it’s a new category between legal information and legal advice.
So actionable legal information, I believe threads that needle between legal advice and legal information and gives people things that they can do to avoid bad consequences down the road.
It’s an upstream solution to the legal problems that people may have.
So we often in the law, in the legal profession occupy a reactive space.

kp.k: Multimodal delivery could broaden public access
kp.d: Nori argues that conventional text-heavy legal information is poorly matched to how people seek help. Beyond chat, he identifies AI-generated video, audio and text messaging as potential ways to reach people in their languages at any time. He claims relatively low costs and limited infrastructure requirements, without supplying cost comparisons or accessibility outcome data.
qs: we lawyers love to put text on screens. Nobody else likes that, right?

You can make videos, you can make audio content, you can send text messages to people, you can reach them wherever they are in whatever language they speak, 24 hours a day, seven days a week, 365 days a year, and the cost is relatively low.
This isn’t something that requires you to overhaul your tech stack or hire a bunch of new people or spend a lot of money.

kp.k: Accuracy concerns require verification and managed experimentation
kp.d: Colpoys reports that accuracy was the leading concern in an October survey of Illinois legal aid lawyers and staff: 70% of all respondents expressed concern; the transcript supplies no respondent count. She recommends change management and early-adopter pilots. Nori argues that practitioners need not understand AI's internal mechanics but must test and verify accuracy for the intended purpose, advocating small steps with measurable, verifiable progress.
qs: So 70% of all respondents said that they were concerned about the accuracy of AI tools.
We need to create a coalition of the willing people who are willing to try things out, get started, pilot solutions, just get going.
What we have to do is trust it, test it, verify it, make sure that it’s accurate for the purpose that we’re using it for.
We have to think in terms of baby steps and progress that is measurable and verifiable and we can bring everyone along with us.

kp.k: Unmet need reframes acceptable AI risk
kp.d: Nori recommends comparing AI assistance with the absence of help rather than perfect legal service. His example of a tool being '90% good' is illustrative, not a measured accuracy result. He asserts that 92% of Americans' civil legal problems go unaddressed, without giving underlying study details. Moon adds that people can already seek advice from general-purpose ChatGPT outside lawyers' control and argues for shaping the quality of that experience.
qs: Instead, don’t compare these tools to the perfect, compare them to what’s available right now to people.
And a tool that’s 90% good looks pretty great compared to zero, it doesn’t look that great compared to 100.
92% of Americans civil legal problems are going unaddressed, 92%.
Any person can log into chat GPT and seek legal help and seek legal advice.

kp.k: Corporate billing disruption is predicted, not demonstrated
kp.d: Nori predicts severe disruption to corporate law and the billable hour. He contrasts associates spending 20, 30 or a hundred hours on a question with AI answering a similar question in 45 seconds, but supplies no supporting benchmark or comparison of output quality. He argues that the same time compression threatening hourly revenue creates capacity opportunities for legal services.
qs: One thing that I think is going to happen is corporate America is going to be decimated corporate law by ai.
they spend 20 hours, 30 hours, a hundred hours on a legal question, guess how long it takes AI to answer a similar legal question? 45 seconds.
The same tools that make the billable hour irrelevant free us from the type of work that takes up all our time and we can do so much more.

kp.k: AI augmentation could improve practitioner wellbeing
kp.d: Colpoys presents mental-health improvement as an opportunity: AI could handle forms and repetitive administrative work while lawyers retain counseling, collaboration and trial work, potentially gaining family time. Nori supports this with his observation of unhappiness and departures without other jobs secured, attributing demoralization partly to tedious work and turning people away. Neither speaker reports measured wellbeing effects from AI.
qs: But I really think this is an opportunity for us to help improve the mental health of legal aid lawyers
The counseling, the collaboration, the trial work, all of the work that the AI isn’t going to be good at.
And perhaps in what, when we do that, we’ll gain time back, more time with our families, less time at the office or your remote office, whatever that is.
I’ve never seen people quitting without having other jobs lined up before.

kp.d: Nori predicts that AI automation of billing, paperwork and office support will lower overhead by 2030, enabling more solo practitioners and smaller, more nimble legal services groups. He anticipates cheaper, more widely available assistance and recommends neighborhood practices with narrower specialties, such as rent overcharges or repairs, rather than general housing practice. These are future projections and organizational recommendations.
qs: we’re going to see more specialized practice areas. We’re going to see a lot more smaller, more nimble legal services groups pop up.
They don’t have as much overhead with billing and paperwork and office support. All of those things can be automated by ai.
We have to move away from the general model of housing attorney and maybe focus on rent overcharge attorney or repair attorney or holdover, no lease attorney.
it’ll be more widely available, more specialized and cheaper.

kp.k: ChatGPT-generated scenarios envision integrated legal assistance
kp.d: Asked about 2030, Colpoys emphasizes uncertainty and explicitly reports brainstorming suggestions generated by ChatGPT rather than independent findings. The three scenarios she shares are ubiquitous digital legal assistance integrated into everyday platforms, enhanced interactive self-help and personal knowledge bases, and seamless access to lawyers through on-demand consultations or subscriptions.
qs: AI is changing so quickly. It’s really hard for me to think about what it’s going to look like in five years.
It gave me 10 things I’ll share the first three.
we will have ubiquitous digital legal assistance.
Second thing was enhanced self-help resources.
And then the third thing was seamless access to lawyers. So on demand consultations and even subscription models.

kp.k: Efficiency raises funding risks and new staffing needs
kp.d: An audience member asks whether funders might cut budgets and replace 10 attorneys with two plus ChatGPT. Nori treats this as a risk to anticipate, not an observed funding change, and argues for using efficiency to address unmet need rather than reducing headcount; his claim that 10 attorneys can do twice the work is not supported with results here. He anticipates roles maintaining retrieval-augmented bots' knowledge bases and researching community needs, alongside new grant types. Moon separately calls for funding value and service rather than hours. Colpoys identifies Illinois IOLTA and New York IOLA funding as supporting the initiatives discussed.
qs: Why can’t you hire two attorneys and have chat GPT, do the rest of your work?
10 attorneys can now do twice as much work. We don’t need fewer attorneys. We need to be able to equip those attorneys to do more.

you’re going to need people to maintain that knowledge base and update the information and go out into the community and find out what the needs are so that the knowledge base is accurate and up to date.
it’s rethinking how we acknowledge and fund value and service that is created for clients, right?
The Lawyers Trust Fund in Illinois and the IOLA program in New York are both funding the work that Satit and I are doing.

kp.k: Legal education is portrayed as lagging AI change
kp.d: Drawing on his tenant-defense clinic teaching, Nori asserts that few law schools are thinking ahead about AI, while naming Cat Moon, Suffolk Law School and Stanford as exceptions. Moon describes her own pedagogical goal as replacing fear with curiosity through experimentation. These are practitioner assessments and teaching recommendations, not a systematic survey of legal education.
qs: But very few people in law schools, in the legal academic world are really thinking ahead about what’s coming.
They’re not doing that much other than people like Cat Moon and others, people at Suffolk Law School and Stanford.
What I strive to do with my students is replace that fear with curiosity.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Nori and Colpoys argue that AI can reduce routine legal-aid work, expand service capacity and leave lawyers more time for distinctly human work.
pts.d: Nori identifies intake, triage, translation, filing and public-facing information as burdens that AI can help address, allowing lawyers to concentrate on substantive problems. Colpoys anticipates improved mental health and potentially more personal time through assistance with forms and other repetitive tasks. These are proposed benefits, not reported results from a measured deployment.

pts.k: Nori presents Roxanne as a direct-to-tenant tool for earlier intervention in housing problems and predicts broader, inexpensive, multilingual access through AI.
pts.d: Roxanne provides natural-language responses about housing conditions. Nori calls its output 'actionable legal information' and believes this occupies a space between information and advice; this is his interpretation, not an established legal determination stated in the transcript. He argues that earlier access could prevent downstream problems and that AI can distribute information through chat, video, audio and text at relatively low cost.

pts.k: Nori predicts severe disruption of corporate law's hourly billing model, while treating the same efficiency gains as an opportunity for legal aid.
pts.d: He argues that AI's speed in answering legal questions will undermine billing based on associate hours. His language predicts imminent structural disruption rather than merely incremental efficiency. He contrasts corporate law's revenue problem with legal aid's opportunity to help more people.

pts.k: Nori predicts more small, specialized legal-service providers and affordable solo practices by 2030.
pts.d: He links automation of billing, paperwork and office support to lower overhead, more viable solo practices, smaller legal-services groups and greater specialization. He expects consumers to receive more options at lower cost and practitioners to develop deeper expertise.

pts.k: Colpoys expects early-adopter pilots and visible successes to encourage wider adoption.
pts.d: She proposes a coalition of willing users, experimentation and peer learning as mechanisms for overcoming organizational resistance. This is a change-management expectation rather than a demonstrated diffusion outcome.

pts.k: Nori argues that AI should expand legal-aid capacity rather than justify fewer lawyers, and predicts new knowledge-maintenance roles.
pts.d: Responding to a hypothetical concern about funding cuts, Nori argues for retaining lawyers, equipping them to serve more people and seeking new types of grants. He predicts that knowledge-base-backed bots will require maintenance, updating and community-needs research. The funding-cut scenario is a question posed to him, not a reported funding decision.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Nori's capacity and wellbeing arguments draw chiefly on professional experience and unmet-need assertions.
pts.d: Nori cites 22 years in New York City legal services, approximately 1,000 clients represented and more than 10,000 people turned away. He estimates that procedural 'how' questions consume over half of time and energy and describes demoralization and departures. He also invokes a 92% unmet-civil-need figure without identifying its source or defining its population in the transcript. These support his rationale for adoption, not a measured AI impact.

pts.k: Colpoys reports survey evidence of accuracy concerns, but not measured AI accuracy or service improvements.
pts.d: An October survey of Illinois legal-aid lawyers and staff found that 70% of respondents were concerned about accuracy, described as their leading concern. The transcript does not supply sample size, response rate or detailed methodology. Colpoys also describes discovery discussions with most of the Lawyers Trust Fund's 55 grantees and baseline collection; these inform adoption support rather than establish AI performance.

pts.k: Roxanne is a concrete deployment example, while the numerical speed and capacity claims are not accompanied by benchmarks.
pts.d: Nori describes a recently launched product but gives no user outcomes, accuracy results or evidence of prevented housing harms. His comparison of many associate hours with a 45-second AI answer and his suggestion that ten attorneys can do twice as much work have no stated measurement basis. His '90% good' comparison is a rhetorical illustration of evaluating help against no help, not a reported model error rate.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current deployment claims concern early 2025, while Nori's market-structure forecast explicitly targets 2030.
pts.d: Nori says Roxanne launched on January 7 after 13 months of work and had been available for only a week. Corporate-law disruption is framed as imminent without a dated forecast. Specialization, lower overhead and wider consumer choice are explicitly discussed as a five-year vision for 2030. Colpoys cautions that five-year forecasting is difficult; the digital-assistance, self-help and subscription ideas she then relays are explicitly attributed to ChatGPT, not presented as independently developed findings.

pts.k: Benefits are conditioned on adoption support, purpose-specific checking, incremental implementation and navigating consumer-facing risks.
pts.d: Colpoys emphasizes change management and accuracy concerns. Nori acknowledges unauthorized-practice, accuracy and trust issues for direct consumer tools and calls for testing and human verification before purpose-specific reliance. He advocates incremental, measurable progress rather than immediate wholesale replacement. Funding outcomes remain uncertain, and he explicitly acknowledges not having all the answers.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: People unable to obtain civil legal help, especially New York City tenants with repair problems, are the principal intended beneficiaries.
pts.d: Nori highlights tenants whose non-eviction problems receive little attention because lawyers prioritize eviction emergencies. Roxanne offers them information directly rather than requiring a lawyer-mediated interaction. His broader access-to-justice argument concerns people otherwise turned away; the proposed benefit is earlier assistance and prevention, not enterprise cost savings.

pts.k: Legal-aid lawyers, smaller providers, corporate-law associates, funders and new support workers face different proposed changes.
pts.d: For legal-aid lawyers, the speakers favor augmentation: less routine work, greater capacity and potentially improved wellbeing. Nori predicts more specialization and viable small practices, with cheaper options for consumers. Corporate-law associates' time-intensive work and firms' hourly revenues are portrayed as vulnerable. Funders may need to support new work arrangements, including staff who maintain bot knowledge bases and assess community needs.
